topics.summary: Doors, scissors, arms and legs all bend or open by turning one part about a point, and the chapter asks how to name and measure that turn.

content.text: In this chapter, we will explore some of the most basic ideas of geometry including points, lines, rays, line segments and angles. These ideas form the building blocks of 'plane geometry', and will help us in understanding more advanced topics in geometry such as the construction and analysis of different shapes.

content.text:
1. Look at the dancing figures on the chapter page and at a door, a pair of scissors and your own arm. Before reading on, guess: what do they all do that a plain straight stick does not?
2. Each one has two parts joined at one point, and one part can turn about that point.
3. When the turn is small the parts stay close, and when it is big they open wide. How can we name that turn, compare two of them and measure one? That is what this chapter finds out.

content.text:
Mark a dot on the paper with a sharp tip of a pencil. The sharper the tip, the thinner will be the dot. This tiny dot will give you an idea of a point. A point determines a precise location, but it has no length, breadth or height. Some models for a point are given below.
If you mark three points on a piece of paper, you may be required to distinguish these three points. For this purpose, each of the three points may be denoted by a single capital letter such as Z, P and T. These points are read as 'Point Z', 'Point P' and 'Point T'. Of course, the dots represent precise locations and must be imagined to be invisibly thin.
Fold a piece of paper and unfold it. Do you see a crease? This gives the idea of a line segment. It has two end points, A and B.

content.text:
Mark any two points A and B on a sheet of paper. Try to connect A to B by various routes (Fig. 2.1).
What is the shortest route from A to B? This shortest path from Point A to Point B (including A and B) as shown here is called the line segment from A to B. It is denoted by either AB (bar over letters) or BA (bar over letters). The points A and B are called the end points of the line segment AB.

source: Draw a rough figure and write labels appropriately to illustrate each of the following: OP and OQ (lines) meet at O. XY (ray) and PQ (line) intersect at point M. Line l contains points E and F but not point D. Point P lies on AB.
never_show: the four finished figures together, before the answer beat
maths_rules: A line is drawn with an arrowhead at both sides, a ray with a dot at its start and one arrowhead, and a line segment with a dot at each end.
OP and OQ are lines meeting at O, so draw two lines that cross, label the crossing O, and put P on one line and Q on the other.
The ray XY starts at X, and it crosses the line PQ at M, so M is on both.
The line l contains E and F, so both are on it, and D is placed away from the line.
P lies on the segment AB, so P is a point between the end points A and B.
video_script.payoff_line: All four figures are drawn and labelled

final_answer.value: (a) two lines crossing at O with P on one and Q on the other; (b) ray XY and line PQ crossing at M; (c) line l through E and F with D off the line; (d) P between A and B on the segment AB
final_answer.spoken: two lines cross at O, with P on one and Q on the other. The ray X Y and the line P Q cross at M. The line L passes through E and F but misses D. The point P lies between eigh and B on the segment eigh B

diagram_spec.manim_description: On a plain BG canvas (16:9) draw four panels in a 2 x 2 grid in reading order, with panel centres a (-4.0, 2.25), b (4.0, 2.25), c (-4.0, -2.25), d (4.0, -2.25) (positions below are local to each panel centre). Draw every line, ray, segment and dot in ANSWER with 3 px strokes and filled dots of radius 0.08, and every letter in INK. Panel a: a horizontal line from (-3.0, 0) to (3.0, 0) with an arrowhead at both ends, and a second line from (-1.8, -1.8) to (1.8, 1.8) with an arrowhead at both ends; they cross at O (0, 0). Dots and letters: O at (0, 0) with the letter at offset (0.25, -0.3); P on the slanted line at (1.2, 1.2) with the letter at offset (-0.25, 0.25); Q on the horizontal line at (2.0, 0) with the letter at offset (0, -0.3). Panel b: a line PQ from (-2.9, -0.725) to (2.9, 0.725) with an arrowhead at both ends, and a ray XY that starts at the dot X (-1.5, 0.9), passes through M (0, 0) and Y (1.5, -0.9) and ends at the tip (2.4, -1.44) with ONE arrowhead at the tip and no arrowhead at X. Dots at X, M, Y, P (-2.0, -0.5) and Q (2.0, 0.5). Letters: X at offset (-0.15, 0.3), M at (0, -0.35), Y at (0, -0.3), P at (0, -0.3), Q at (0, 0.3). Panel c: a horizontal line from (-3.0, 0.3) to (3.0, 0.3) with an arrowhead at both ends, the italic letter l in INK at (3.35, 0.3); dots E (-1.6, 0.3) and F (0.8, 0.3) on the line with their letters at offset (0, 0.35); a separate dot D at (-0.4, -1.0), clearly off the line, with its letter at offset (0.3, 0). Panel d: a horizontal segment from A (-2.8, 0) to B (2.8, 0) with no arrowheads; dots at A, P (-1.06, 0) and B, with the letter P at offset (0, 0.35) and the letters A and B at offset (0, -0.35). Part letters (the LP answer names the figures by letter): write (a), (b), (c), (d) in INK, 48 px (0.4 unit), each centred on its anchor, canvas units, origin at the canvas centre, x right, y up, 1 unit = 120 px: (a) at (-7.2, 4); (b) at (0.8, 4); (c) at (-7.2, -0.5); (d) at (0.8, -0.5). Each letter sits just outside the top-left corner of its panel, clear of every line and label.

source: A pair of scissors has two blades. When we open them (or 'turn them') to cut something, the blades form an angle. Identify the arms and the vertex of the angle.
never_show: the screw named as the vertex, before the answer beat
video_script.wrong_move: Kiko says the vertex is where the blades cut because that is where the cutting happens. The cutting place is shown in three different places while the screw stays at one place, so the bubble is struck.
maths_rules: An angle is formed by two rays with a common starting point; the rays are the arms and the starting point is the vertex.
In scissors the two blades turn, so each blade lies along an arm.
The two blades are joined at the screw, so both arms start there and the screw is the vertex.
Slip: the cutting place moves along the blades when the scissors close, so it is not the vertex.

More turn means a greater angle, so the angle in Case two is greater.

maths_rules: An angle has two arms that start at one vertex, and its size is the amount of turn about the vertex.
In a compass one leg is held still and the other leg is turned about the joint, so an angle opens up.
The same holds for scissors and spectacles: one part is held still and the other is turned about the hinge.
So each angle is formed when one arm is turned about the vertex with respect to the other.
Slip: the gap between the tips depends on the arm length, so it is not the angle.

topics.summary: An angle is two rays from one point; its size is the amount one arm turns about the vertex, and the name puts the vertex in the middle.

content.text:
An angle is formed by two rays having a common starting point. Here is an angle formed by rays BD and BE where B is the common starting point (Fig. 2.8).
The point B is called the vertex of the angle, and the rays BD and BE are called the arms of the angle. How can we name this angle? We can simply use the vertex and say that it is the Angle B. To be clearer, we use a point on each of the arms together with the vertex to name the angle. In this case, we name the angle as Angle DBE or Angle EBD. The word angle can be replaced by the symbol '∠', i.e., ∠DBE or ∠EBD. Note that in specifying the angle, the vertex is always written as the middle letter.
To indicate an angle, we use a small curve at the vertex (refer to Fig. 2.9).
Vidya has just opened her book. Let us observe her opening the cover of the book in different scenarios.
Do you see angles being made in each of these cases? Can you mark their arms and vertex?
Let's look at some other examples where angles arise in real life by rotation or turn:
In a compass or divider, we turn the arms to form an angle. The vertex is the point where the two arms are joined. Identify the arms and vertex of the angle.
A pair of scissors has two blades. When we open them (or 'turn them') to cut something, the blades form an angle. Identify the arms and the vertex of the angle.
Look at the pictures of spectacles, wallet and other common objects. Identify the angles in them by marking out their arms and vertices.

content.text:
Worked example: In a compass or divider, we turn the arms to form an angle. The vertex is the point where the two arms are joined. Identify the arms and vertex of the angle.
1. The two legs are the arms.
2. The joint where they meet is the vertex.
Answer: The two legs of the compass are the arms; the vertex is the joint (hinge) at the top where the arms are joined.

Worked example: A pair of scissors has two blades. When we open them (or 'turn them') to cut something, the blades form an angle. Identify the arms and the vertex of the angle.
1. The blades are the arms.
2. The pivot screw is the vertex.
Answer: The two blades are the arms; the vertex is the screw/pivot where the blades are joined.

concepts.concept_name: Arms and vertex in everyday things

content.text:
Worked example: Look at the pictures of spectacles, wallet and other common objects (a stapler, a hinged box, a box with an open flap). Identify the angles in them by marking out their arms and vertices.
1. Find the two parts that turn about a hinge.
2. Those parts are the arms; the hinge is the vertex.
Answer: Each object has two parts joined at a hinge; the two parts are the arms and the hinge is the vertex (e.g., spectacles: a temple (side arm) and the frame; wallet: the two halves; stapler: the top and base; box: lid and box).

content.text:
Which angle is greater, the angle in Case 1 or the angle in Case 2?
Just as we talk about the size of a line based on its length, we also talk about the size of an angle based on its amount of rotation.
So, the angle in Case 2 is greater as in this case she needs to rotate the cover more. Similarly, the angle in Case 3 is even larger than that of Case 2, because there is even more rotation, and Cases 4, 5, and 6 are successively larger angles with more and more rotation.
The size of an angle is the amount of rotation or turn that is needed about the vertex to move the first ray to the second ray. (boxed definition with Fig. 2.9)
Do you see how these angles are formed by turning one arm with respect to the other?

So, the angle in Case 2 is greater as in this case she needs to rotate the cover more. Similarly, the angle in Case 3 is even larger than that of Case 2, because there is even more rotation, and Cases 4, 5, and 6 are successively larger angles with more and more rotation.
The size of an angle is the amount of rotation or turn that is needed about the vertex to move the first ray to the second ray. (boxed definition with Fig. 2.9)

source: Mark any three points on your paper that are not on one line. Label them A, B, C. Draw all possible lines going through pairs of these points. How many lines do you get? Name them. The points are not on one line, so at each point two of the lines meet and make an angle.
The angle at B is ABC, the angle at C is BCA, and the angle at A is CAB, with the vertex as the middle letter.
So there are 3 lines and 3 angles.

video_script.design: One idea: six pairs give six lines, and each of the four points is the vertex of three angles. The four points stay on the board, the lines are drawn one at a time, and the angles are named point by point. The method is the same way as the examples in the book on the arms and the vertex of an angle.
source: Now mark any four points on your paper so that no three of them are on one line. Label them A, B, C, D. Draw all possible lines going through pairs of these points. How many lines do you get? Name them. How many angles can you name using A, B, C, D? Write them all down, and mark each of them with a curve as in Fig. 2.9.
never_show: the count of the lines or of the angles, before the answer beat
maths_rules: A line is drawn through each pair of the four points: AB, AC, AD, BC, BD and CD, which makes 6 lines.
No three points are on one line, so every pair gives its own line, and BA is the same line as AB.
At A the other points B, C and D, taken two at a time, give the angles BAC, CAD and BAD.
At each of the four points there are 3 angles in the same way, so there are 4 times 3, which is 12 angles.
The vertex is the middle letter in the name of each angle.

content.text:
$1$. At $P$ there are three rays, $PA$, $PB$, $PC$.
$2$. So there are three different angles at $P$.
$3$. $\angle P$ alone cannot tell which one; use points on both arms.
Answer: Three angles share the vertex $P$: $\angle APB$, $\angle BPC$ and $\angle APC$. Naming one as $\angle P$ would not say which of them is meant, so we must name a point on each arm.

media.context: Class 6 NCERT Ganita Prakash ch 2 'Lines and Angles' (Comparing Angles and Special Angles). Lay one angle over the other. See which is greater. Viral_V3 tool, ported from its standalone HTML.
media.description: Which Angle Is Greater?. Lay one angle over the other. See which is greater. Authored rounds, no modes and no question bank: the child acts on the board, then answers; a header with points, hint, sound and home; a task card with Check; a message pill; step dots; Next / Finish; a finish screen with stars. Everything starts raw and changes only when the child acts. English, Hindi and Gujarati.

content.text:
Look at these animals opening their mouths. Do you see any angles here? If yes, mark the arms and vertex of each one. Some mouths are open wider than others; the more the turning of the jaws, the larger the angle! Can you arrange the angles in this picture from smallest to largest?
Here are some angles. Label each of the angles. How will you compare them?
Draw a few more angles; label them and compare.
Any two angles can be compared by placing them one over the other, i.e., by superimposition. While superimposing, the vertices of the angles must overlap.
After superimposition, it becomes clear which angle is smaller and which is larger.
The picture shows the two angles superimposed. It is now clear that ∠PQR is larger than ∠ABC.

Answer: Yes, each mouth makes an angle (the two jaws are the arms; the hinge of the jaws is the vertex). Arrange them by how wide each mouth is open; the crocodile's looks widest.

content.text:
Equal angles. Now consider ∠AOB and ∠XOY in the figure. Which is greater?
The corners of both of these angles match and the arms overlap with each other, i.e., OA and OX, and OB and OY overlap. So, the angles are equal in size.
The reason these angles are considered to be equal in size is because when we visualise each of these angles as being formed out of rotation, we can see that there is an equal amount of rotation needed to move OB to OA and OY to OX.
From the point of view of superimposition, when two angles are superimposed, and the common vertex and the two rays of both angles lie on top of each other, then the sizes of the angles are equal.
Where else do we use superimposition to compare?

concepts.concept_name: Equal angles, whatever the arm length

content.text:
Two cranes are arguing about who can open their mouth wider, i.e., who is making a bigger angle.
Let us first draw their angles. How do we know which one is bigger? As seen before, one could trace these angles, superimpose them and then check. But can we do it without superimposition?
Suppose we have a transparent circle which can be moved and placed on figures. Can we use this for comparison?
Let us place the circular paper on the angle made by the first crane. The circle is placed in such a way that its centre is on the vertex of the angle. Let us mark the points A and B on the edge circle at the points where the arms of the angle pass through the circle.
Can we use this to find out if this angle is greater than, or equal to or smaller than the angle made by the second crane?
Let us place it on the angle made by the second crane so that the vertex coincides with the centre of the circle and one of the arms passes through OA.
Can you now tell which angle is bigger?
Which crane was making the bigger angle?
If you can make a circular piece of transparent paper, try this method to compare the angles in Fig. 2.10 with each other.

The circle is then placed on the second crane's angle with the vertex at the centre and one arm through OA. Can you now tell which angle is bigger?
{{DIAGRAM:M2.S8.T8.C45.IMG1}}
1. Match one arm of each angle with OA.
2. Compare the other end points on the circle (B and Y).
3. A farther end point means a bigger angle.
Answer: Compare where the second arm meets the circle, at Y, with the point B. If Y is beyond B the second angle is bigger, if Y falls on B they are equal, and if Y falls short of B it is smaller. Here Y is very close to B, so the two angles are nearly equal.

content.text: Is it always easy to compare two angles?
content.q_figure: Four angles drawn side by side with different openings and different directions, each marked with a small curve at its vertex.
content.question: Is it always easy to compare two angles?
content.book_number: Comparing Angles: is it always easy?
content.question_tex: Is it always easy to compare two angles?
content.publication_text: Is it always easy to compare two angles?

content.text:
$1$. Angles with nearly the same opening look alike.
$2$. We need superimposition (or measuring) to be sure.
Answer: No. It is not always easy to compare two angles; for example angles of $89$ degrees and $91$ degrees cannot be compared without measuring or overlapping. For the given figures, comparison is easy.

content.text:
{{DIAGRAM:M2.S10.T10.C53.IMG1}}
$1$. Fold the sheet and mark the crease.
$2$. Name the four angles between the crease and the sides.
$3$. Compare by superimposition or folding.
Answer: Example from the book: a slanting crease $EF$ from $E$ on one long side to $F$ on the opposite side gives the angles $\angle AEF$, $\angle BEF$, $\angle DFE$, $\angle CFE$. $\angle AEF$ and $\angle CFE$ are larger than $\angle BEF$ and $\angle DFE$. Try more cases; the largest and smallest depend on the folds you make.

content.text:

content.text:
Let us make 'rotating arms' using two paper straws and a paper clip by following these steps:
1. Take two paper straws and a paper clip. 2. Insert the straws into the arms of the paper clip. 3. Your rotating arm is ready!
Make several 'rotating arms' with different angles between the arms. Arrange the angles you have made from smallest to largest by comparing and using superimposition.
Passing through a slit: Collect a number of rotating arms with different angles; do not rotate any of the rotating arms during this activity.
Take a cardboard and make an angle-shaped slit as shown below by tracing and cutting out the shape of one of the rotating arms.
Now, shuffle and mix up all the rotating arms. Can you identify which of the rotating arms will pass through the slit?
The correct one can be found by placing each of the rotating arms over the slit. Let us do this for some of the rotating arms:
Captions: Slit angle is greater than the arms' angle. The arms will not go through the slit. | Slit angle is less than the arms' angle. The arms will not go through the slit. | Slit angle is equal to the arms' angle. The arms will go through the slit.
Only the pair of rotating arms where the angle is equal to that of the slit passes through the slit. Note that the possibility of passing through the slit depends only on the angle between the rotating arms and not on their lengths (as long as they are shorter than the length of the slit).

content.text:
Worked example: Collect a number of rotating arms with different angles (do not rotate any of them). Take a cardboard and make an angle-shaped slit by tracing and cutting out the shape of one of the rotating arms. Now shuffle and mix up all the rotating arms. Can you identify which of the rotating arms will pass through the slit?
1. Place an arm over the slit.
2. If the slit angle is greater than the arms' angle, the arms will not go through.
3. If the slit angle is less than the arms' angle, the arms will not go through.
4. If equal, the arms go through.
Answer: Only the arm whose angle is equal to the slit's angle passes through; place each over the slit to find it. Passing through depends only on the angle, not on the arms' lengths (as long as they are shorter than the slit).

1. Predict first: a girl snips the ends off the arms of a V-shaped rotating arm. Is the angle now smaller?
2. The two arms still meet at the same vertex with the same turn between them, so the angle is unchanged.
3. To reduce the angle, turn one arm towards the other. The size of an angle is the amount of turn, not the length of the arms.

content.text:
Let us go back to Vidya's notebook and observe her opening the cover of the book in different scenarios.
She makes a full turn of the cover when she has to write while holding the book in her hand.
She makes a half turn of the cover when she has to open it on her table. In this case, observe the arms of the angle formed. They lie in a straight line. Such an angle is called a straight angle.
Let us consider a straight angle ∠AOB. Observe that any ray OC divides it into two angles, ∠AOC and ∠COB.
Is it possible to draw OC such that the two angles are equal to each other in size?
We can try to solve this problem using a piece of paper. Recall that when a fold is made, it creates a crease which is straight.
Take a rectangular piece of paper and on one of its sides, mark the straight angle AOB. By folding, try to get a line (crease) passing through O that divides ∠AOB into two equal angles.
How can it be done?
Fold the paper such that OB overlaps with OA. Observe the crease and the two angles formed.
Justify why the two angles are equal. Is there a way to superimpose and check? Can this superimposition be done by folding?
Each of these equal angles formed are called right angles. So, a straight angle contains two right angles.

content.text:
If a straight angle is formed by half of a full turn, how much of a full turn will form a right angle?
Observe that a right angle resembles the shape of an 'L'. An angle is a right angle only if it is exactly half of a straight angle. Two lines that meet at right angles are called perpendicular lines.

$2$. Half of half a turn $= \frac{1}{4}$ of a full turn.
Answer: $\frac{1}{4}$ of a full turn (one quarter turn).

topics.summary: Compared with a right angle, an angle is acute if it is smaller, right if it fits exactly, and obtuse if it is bigger but less than a straight angle.

content.text:
Angles are classified in three groups as shown below. Right angles are shown in the second group. What could be the common feature of the other two groups?
In the first group, all angles are less than a right angle or in other words, less than a quarter turn. Such angles are called acute angles.
In the third group, all angles are greater than a right angle but less than a straight angle. The turning is more than a quarter turn and less than a half turn. Such angles are called obtuse angles.

content.text:
$1$. A small opening makes a sharp point.

topics.summary: A circle is divided into 360 equal angles of 1 degree, so a full turn is 360°, a straight angle is 180° and a right angle is 90°.

content.text:
We have seen how to compare two angles. But can we actually quantify how big an angle is using a number without having to compare it to another angle?
We saw how various angles can be compared using a circle. Perhaps a circle could be used to assign measures for angles?
To assign precise measures to angles, mathematicians came up with an idea. They divided the angle in the centre of the circle into 360 equal angles or parts. The angle measure of each of these unit parts is 1 degree, which is written as 1°.
This unit part is used to assign measure to any angle: the measure of an angle is the number of 1° unit parts it contains inside it. For example, see this figure:
It contains 30 units of 1° angle and so we say that its angle measure is 30°.
Measures of different angles: What is the measure of a full turn in degrees? As we have taken it to contain 360 degrees, its measure is 360°.
What is the measure of a straight angle in degrees? A straight angle is half of a full turn. As a full-turn is 360°, a half turn is 180°.
What is the measure of a right angle in degrees? Two right angles together form a straight angle. As a straight angle measures 180°, a right angle measures 90°.

2. Each equal part is a unit angle of 1 degree, written 1°. The measure of an angle is the number of 1° parts in it.
3. A full turn is 360°. A straight angle is half of it, 180°, and a right angle is half of that, 90°.

content.text:
A full turn has been divided into 360°. Why 360? The reason why we use 360° today is not fully known. The division of a circle into 360 parts goes back to ancient times. The Rigveda, one of the very oldest texts of humanity going back thousands of years, speaks of a wheel with 360 spokes (Verse 1.164.48). Many ancient calendars, also going back over 3000 years, such as calendars of India, Persia, Babylonia and Egypt, were based on having 360 days in a year. In addition, Babylonian mathematicians frequently used divisions of 60 and 360 due to their use of sexagesimal numbers and counting by 60s.
Perhaps the most important and practical answer for why mathematicians over the years have liked and continued to use 360 degrees is that 360 is the smallest number that can be evenly divided by all numbers up to 10, aside from 7. Thus, one can break up the circle into 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9 or 10 equal parts, and still have a whole number of degrees in each part! Note that 360 is also evenly divisible by 12, the number of months in a year, and by 24, the number of hours in a day. These facts all make the number 360 very useful.
The circle has been divided into 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9 10 and 12 parts below. What are the degree measures of the resulting angles? Write the degree measures down near the indicated angles.

The Rigveda, one of the very oldest texts of humanity going back thousands of years, speaks of a wheel with 360 spokes (Verse 1.164.48). Many ancient calendars, also going back over 3000 years, such as calendars of India, Persia, Babylonia and Egypt, were based on having 360 days in a year. In addition, Babylonian mathematicians frequently used divisions of 60 and 360 due to their use of sexagesimal numbers and counting by 60s.

Perhaps the most important and practical answer for why mathematicians over the years have liked and continued to use 360 degrees is that 360 is the smallest number that can be evenly divided by all numbers up to 10, aside from 7. Thus, one can break up the circle into 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9 or 10 equal parts, and still have a whole number of degrees in each part! Note that 360 is also evenly divisible by 12, the number of months in a year, and by 24, the number of hours in a day. These facts all make the number 360 very useful.
The circle has been divided into 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9 10 and 12 parts below. What are the degree measures of the resulting angles? Write the degree measures down near the indicated angles.

content.text:
1. Predict first: cut a circle into 4 equal parts. How many degrees is each angle at the centre?
2. Divide 360 by the number of parts: 360 ÷ 4 = 90, so each is 90°.
3. 360 divides evenly by 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10 and 12, so it gives whole-number angles for all of these cuts. That is one reason people kept it.

One degree is one of the 360 equal parts of a full turn.
A straight angle is 180 degrees and a right angle is 90 degrees.
Divide 360 by the number of equal parts to get each angle.

content.text:
$1$. A full turn is $360$ degrees; a straight angle is half a full turn, so $180$ degrees
$2$. Two right angles form a straight angle, so a right angle is $180 \div 2 = 90$ degrees
Answer: Straight angle $= 180$ degrees; right angle $= 90$ degrees.

media.description: Six rays leave the centre of a protractor, and the scale that starts at zero on the first ray gives a reading for each of the others. Angles with the first ray are read directly, and every other angle is found by subtracting two readings. Keeko's doubt, that the two readings should be added, is broken by showing a part that would be bigger than its whole.

content.text:
How can we measure other angles in degrees? It is for this purpose that we have a tool called a protractor that is either a circle divided into 360 equal parts as shown in Fig. 2.12 (on page 32), or a half circle divided into 180 equal parts.
Here is a protractor. Do you see the straight angle at the center divided into 180 units of 1 degree? Only part of the lines dividing the straight angle are visible, though!
Starting from the marking on the rightmost point of the base, there is a long mark for every 10°. From every such long mark, there is a medium sized mark after 5°.
This is a protractor that you find in your geometry box. It would appear similar to the protractor above except that there are numbers written on it. Will these make it easier to read the angles?
There are two sets of numbers on the protractor: one increasing from right to left and the other increasing from left to right. Why does it include two sets of numbers?

content.text:
1. Predict first: a protractor shows two rows of numbers, one growing left to right and one right to left. Why have both?
2. The marks are 1° units, with a long mark every 10° and a medium one every 5°. You can count in 5s and 10s instead of ones.
3. The two scales let you start from 0 on whichever arm is the base arm, left or right.

{{DIAGRAM:M3.S19.T19.C95.IMG2}}
1. One scale starts at 0 on the right and increases anticlockwise
2. The other starts at 0 on the left and increases clockwise
3. Use the scale whose 0 lies on the arm you chose as the base
Answer: Open-ended. The two scales let you read from either arm as the 0 line (base arm on the right or on the left).

content.text:
{{DIAGRAM:M3.S20.T20.C100.IMG1}}
$1$. The vertex $A$ is at the centre of the protractor, so the units of $1$ degree between two arms give the angle.
$2$. The long marks come every $10\text{ units}$ and the medium marks $5\text{ units}$ after each long mark, so we can count in $10s$ or in $5s$.
$3$. $\angle KAL$ holds $3$ long steps: $3 \times 10^\circ = 30^\circ$.
$4$. $\angle WAL$ holds $5$ long steps: $5 \times 10^\circ = 50^\circ$.
$5$. $\angle TAK$ holds $12$ long steps: $12 \times 10^\circ = 120^\circ$.
$6$. Check by counting in $5s$: $6 \times 5^\circ = 30^\circ$, $10 \times 5^\circ = 50^\circ$ and $24 \times 5^\circ = 120^\circ$, the same as the counts in $10s$.
Answer: $(a)$: $\angle KAL = 30^\circ$, $(b)$: $\angle WAL = 50^\circ$, $(c)$: $\angle TAK = 120^\circ$. Yes, it is possible to count in $5s$ or $10s$.
steps: The vertex A is at the centre of the protractor, so the units of 1 degree between two arms give the angle.
The long marks come every 10 units and the medium marks 5 units after each long mark, so we can count in 10s or in 5s.
∠KAL holds 3 long steps: 3 × 10° = 30°.
∠WAL holds 5 long steps: 5 × 10° = 50°.
∠TAK holds 12 long steps: 12 × 10° = 120°.
Check by counting in 5s: 6 × 5° = 30°, 10 × 5° = 50° and 24 × 5° = 120°, the same as the counts in 10s.
content.answer: a. ∠KAL = 30°, b. ∠WAL = 50°, c. ∠TAK = 120°. Yes, it is possible to count in 5s or 10s.
content.question: Write the measures of the following angles: a. ∠KAL b. ∠WAL c. ∠TAK. (Worked in the book for a: the vertex coincides with the centre of the protractor, so the number of units of 1 degree between KA and AL gives ∠KAL = 30°. Follow-up: Making use of the medium sized and large sized marks, is it possible to count the number of units in 5s or 10s?) a) ∠KAL b) ∠WAL c) ∠TAK
steps_tex:
{{DIAGRAM:M3.S20.T20.C100.IMG1}}
The vertex $A$ is at the centre of the protractor, so the units of $1$ degree between two arms give the angle.
The long marks come every $10\text{ units}$ and the medium marks $5\text{ units}$ after each long mark, so we can count in $10s$ or in $5s$.
$\angle KAL$ holds $3$ long steps: $3 \times 10^\circ = 30^\circ$.
$\angle WAL$ holds $5$ long steps: $5 \times 10^\circ = 50^\circ$.
$\angle TAK$ holds $12$ long steps: $12 \times 10^\circ = 120^\circ$.
Check by counting in $5s$: $6 \times 5^\circ = 30^\circ$, $10 \times 5^\circ = 50^\circ$ and $24 \times 5^\circ = 120^\circ$, the same as the counts in $10s$.

diagram_spec.manim_description: Draw a geometry-box protractor as printed on the NCERT page. Its centre O is the middle of its straight base and its outer radius is R; every size below is a fraction of R, with x to the right, y upward and O at the origin. Body: a half-disc of radius R (the part with y >= 0) filled CELL_FILL with a GUIDE outline of 2 px; under the base line a flat strip from x = -R to x = +R and from y = 0 down to y = -0.07 R, filled CELL_FILL with a GUIDE outline; the base line y = 0 from x = -0.67 R to x = +0.67 R is drawn in INK 2 px. Centre cut-out: a half-disc of radius 0.25 R centred at O, filled BG, with a GUIDE outline. Tick ring: 181 GUIDE ticks at 0, 1, 2 ... 180 degrees measured anticlockwise from the right end of the base, each pointing inward from the rim radius R: length 0.03 R at every 1 degree, 0.05 R at every multiple of 5 degrees and 0.09 R at every multiple of 10 degrees. Scale arcs: three GUIDE semicircle arcs of radius 0.91 R, 0.79 R and 0.67 R. Outer scale numbers: the 19 numbers 0, 10, 20 ... 180 in INK, each centred at radius 0.85 R and rotated to follow the arc; the outer scale reads 0 at the left end of the base and 180 at the right end, so the number n sits at (180 - n) degrees measured anticlockwise from the right end. Inner scale numbers: the 19 numbers 0, 10, 20 ... 180 in INK, each centred at radius 0.73 R and rotated to follow the arc; the inner scale reads 0 at the right end of the base and 180 at the left end, so the number n sits at n degrees measured anticlockwise from the right end. The number height is 0.065 R. Radial lines: 17 straight GUIDE lines at 10, 20 ... 170 degrees from the right end, each from radius 0.25 R to radius 0.67 R; the 90-degree line is drawn in INK. Rays: from O draw six rays in INK 4 px, each of length 1.30 R with a small filled INK arrowhead (length 0.05 R) at its tip, at these angles measured anticlockwise from the right end of the base: OP at 0 degrees (along the base to the right), OQ at 35 degrees, OR at 95 degrees, OS at 125 degrees, OT at 160 degrees and OU at 180 degrees (along the base to the left), so P, O and U lie on one horizontal straight line. The rays pass over the scales and leave the protractor. Letters: P, Q, R, S, T and U in INK, each centred at distance 1.43 R from O on its own ray, and the letter O in INK centred at (0, -0.17 R). No other text and no angle arcs. Canvas: 1456 x 816 px card, BG white, R = 400 px; centre the drawing so that its bounding box (x from -1.47 R to +1.47 R, y from -0.22 R to +1.47 R) sits in the middle of the card.

video_script.anchor: the book's labelled protractor with the arms OT and OS passing through twenty and fifty five on the outer scale
video_script.design: One idea: take the smaller reading away from the larger on the same set. The ruler picture in the ground beat gives the child the subtraction idea before the protractor returns.
source: Can you use the numbers marked to find the angle without cou
video_script.wrong_move: Kiko adds the two readings and says the angle is seventy five degrees. The angle is only the stretch between the two arms, which holds far fewer than seventy five units, so the bubble is struck.
maths_rules: ground: a pencil with its ends at 14 and 40 on a ruler has length 40 - 14 = 26 units
arms OT and OS pass through 20 and 55 on the same outer set
the angle is the number of 1 degree units between them: 55 - 20 = 35, so the angle is 35 degrees
check: start at 20 and go up 35 units to reach 55
slip: adding gives 75, but 75 is more than the reading 55 itself, and the arms are only 35 units apart
video_script.payoff_line: Fifty five take away twenty gives thirty five degrees

final_answer.spoken: yes, subtraction can be used, and fifty five take away twenty gives thirty five degrees

video_script.substitution: The gap between two readings is treated like the length between two marks on a ruler: take the smaller away from the larger.
video_script.wrong_answer: add twenty and fifty five to get seventy five degrees

diagram_spec.manim_description: Draw a geometry-box protractor as printed on the NCERT page. Its centre O is the middle of its straight base and its outer radius is R; every size below is a fraction of R, with x to the right, y upward and O at the origin. Body: a half-disc of radius R (the part with y >= 0) filled CELL_FILL with a GUIDE outline of 2 px; under the base line a flat strip from x = -R to x = +R and from y = 0 down to y = -0.07 R, filled CELL_FILL with a GUIDE outline; the base line y = 0 from x = -0.67 R to x = +0.67 R is drawn in INK 2 px. Centre cut-out: a half-disc of radius 0.25 R centred at O, filled BG, with a GUIDE outline. Tick ring: 181 GUIDE ticks at 0, 1, 2 ... 180 degrees measured anticlockwise from the right end of the base, each pointing inward from the rim radius R: length 0.03 R at every 1 degree, 0.05 R at every multiple of 5 degrees and 0.09 R at every multiple of 10 degrees. Scale arcs: three GUIDE semicircle arcs of radius 0.91 R, 0.79 R and 0.67 R. Outer scale numbers: the 19 numbers 0, 10, 20 ... 180 in INK, each centred at radius 0.85 R and rotated to follow the arc; the outer scale reads 0 at the left end of the base and 180 at the right end, so the number n sits at (180 - n) degrees measured anticlockwise from the right end. Inner scale numbers: the 19 numbers 0, 10, 20 ... 180 in INK, each centred at radius 0.73 R and rotated to follow the arc; the inner scale reads 0 at the right end of the base and 180 at the left end, so the number n sits at n degrees measured anticlockwise from the right end. The number height is 0.065 R. Radial lines: 17 straight GUIDE lines at 10, 20 ... 170 degrees from the right end, each from radius 0.25 R to radius 0.67 R; the 90-degree line is drawn in INK. Rays: from O draw two rays in INK 4 px, each of length 1.15 R with a small filled INK arrowhead (length 0.05 R) at its tip: OT at 160 degrees and OS at 125 degrees, measured anticlockwise from the right end of the base (so OT crosses the outer scale at the number 20 and OS crosses it at the number 55). Letters: T and S in INK, each centred at distance 1.28 R from O on its own ray, and the letter O in INK centred at (0, -0.17 R). Highlights in FOCUS (3 px, no fill): one circle of radius 0.06 R around the outer-scale number 20 (centre at radius 0.85 R and 160 degrees) and one circle of radius 0.06 R around the outer-scale number 55 (centre at radius 0.85 R and 125 degrees). Answer marks in ANSWER green: an arc of radius 1.03 R from 125 degrees to 160 degrees (3 px) and the label '35°' centred at radius 1.12 R on the direction 142.5 degrees, number height 0.065 R. Canvas: 1456 x 816 px card, BG white, R = 400 px; centre the drawing so that its bounding box (x from -1.40 R to +1.04 R, y from -0.22 R to +1.40 R) sits in the middle of the card.
must_not_show: the other rays P, Q, R, U
accuracy_checks: OT at 160 degrees from the right end passes the outer number 180 - 160 = 20
OS at 125 degrees from the right end passes the outer number 180 - 125 = 55
55 - 20 = 35, and the arc from 125 to 160 degrees is 160 - 125 = 35 degrees

source: Make your own protractor by paper folding. 1. Draw a circle of a convenient radius on a sheet of paper. Cut out the circle. A circle or one full turn is 360°. 2. Fold the circle to get two equal halves and cut it through the crease to get a semicircle. Write '0°' in the bottom right corner of the semicircle. 3. Fold the semi-circular sheet in half to form a quarter circle. 4. Fold the sheet again. 5. Continue with another half fold. 6. Unfold and mark the creases as OB, OC, ..., etc. (2.9 Make your own protractor, pages 37 to 39)
video_script.wrong_move: Kiko says the marks will come out ten degrees apart. Ten degrees apart would need eighteen parts, but three half folds give only eight equal parts, so the bubble is struck.
maths_rules: a full turn is 360 degrees; the first cut gives a semicircle, 360 / 2 = 180 degrees
each half fold halves the last angle: 180 / 2 = 90, 90 / 2 = 45, 45 / 2 = 22.5
three half folds give 2 x 2 x 2 = 8 equal parts of the straight angle, each 22.5 degrees
ten degrees apart would need 180 / 10 = 18 parts, but three folds give 8
video_script.payoff_line: The creases make marks every twenty two point five degrees from zero to one hundred and eighty

final_answer.spoken: the marks are zero, twenty two point five, forty five, sixty seven point five, ninety, one hundred twelve point five, one hundred thirty five, one hundred fifty seven point five and one hundred eighty degrees

video_script.substitution: The book's paper circle, cut into a semicircle and folded in half again and again.
video_script.wrong_answer: the marks will come out ten degrees apart

media.teaching_notes: One idea: each half fold halves the last angle, so three folds make eight equal parts of a straight angle. Watch for children who expect round-number marks.

content.text:
You may have wondered how the different equally spaced markings are made on a protractor. We will now see how we can make some of them!
1. Draw a circle of a convenient radius on a sheet of paper. Cut out the circle (Fig. 2.13). A circle or one full turn is 360°.
2. Fold the circle to get two equal halves and cut it through the crease to get a semicircle. Write '0°' in the bottom right corner of the semicircle.
The measure of half a circle is 1/2 of a full turn. (Fig. 2.14) So, the measure of half a turn = 1/2 of ____ = 180°. Thus, write 180° in the left bottom corner of the semicircle.
3. Fold the semi-circular sheet in half as shown in Fig. 2.15 to form a quarter circle.
The measure of a quarter circle is 1/4 of a full turn. The measure of a 1/4 turn = 1/4 of 360° is ______. Or, the measure of a 1/4 turn = 1/2 of a half turn = 1/2 of 180° is ______. Thus, mark 90° at the top of the semicircle.

1. Predict first: you fold a paper circle in half. Which angle does the half circle show at its centre?
2. A full turn is 360°, so half a turn is half of 360° and measures 180°.
3. Fold the semicircle in half to get a quarter circle. A quarter of 360° is 90°, and half of 180° is also 90°, so write 90° at the top.

content.text:
Worked example: Make your own protractor by paper folding. 1. Draw a circle of a convenient radius on a sheet of paper. Cut out the circle (Fig. 2.13). A circle or one full turn is 360°. 2. Fold the circle to get two equal halves and cut it through the crease to get a semicircle. Write '0°' in the bottom right corner of the semicircle. 3. Fold the semi-circular sheet in half as shown in Fig. 2.15 to form a quarter circle. 4. Fold the sheet again as shown in Figs. 2.16 and 2.17. 5. Continue with another half fold as shown in Fig. 2.18. 6. Unfold and mark the creases as OB, OC, ..., etc., as shown in Fig. 2.19 and Fig. 2.20.
{{DIAGRAM:M3.S22.T22.C107.IMG2}}
1. Circle = 360°; half fold gives 180° (write 180° at left bottom corner)

Continue with another half fold as shown in Fig. 2.18. 6. Unfold and mark the creases as OB, OC, ..., etc., as shown in Fig. 2.19 and Fig. 2.20.

content.text:
$1$. Place the centre of the protractor exactly on the vertex $H$.
$2$. Turn the protractor until one arm lies along the $0$ line, and read the scale that starts at that $0$.
$3$. Follow the other arm out to the scale: the first figure reads $47^\circ$.
$4$. Do the same for the second figure: it reads $23^\circ$.
$5$. Do the same for the third figure: it reads $108^\circ$.
$6$. Check with a right angle $(90^\circ)$: $47^\circ$ and $23^\circ$ are less than $90^\circ$, and $108^\circ$ is more than $90^\circ$.
Answer: First figure: $47^\circ$. Second figure: $23^\circ$. Third figure: $108^\circ$.

content.text:
$1$. Sample answer: choose a corner of the board and put the centre of the protractor exactly on that corner.
$2$. Turn the protractor until one edge lies along the $0$ line, and read the scale that starts at that $0$.
$3$. Follow the other edge out to the scale and read the number: the corner of a board or a book reads about $90^\circ$.
$4$. Do the same for the door and for a window: each gives its own reading, and a door opened a little reads less than $90^\circ$.
Answer: Open-ended (corners of the board, door, books, etc.).

$3$. Measure $\angle BXE$ and $\angle CXE$ in the same way: $\angle BXE = 115^\circ$ and $\angle CXE = 85^\circ$.
$4$. Find $\angle BXC$ by subtraction: $\angle BXC = \angle BXE - \angle CXE = 115^\circ - 85^\circ = 30^\circ$.

Answer: $\angle BXE = 115^\circ$, $\angle CXE = 85^\circ$, $\angle AXB = 65^\circ$, $\angle BXC = 30^\circ$

$1$. Put the centre of the protractor exactly on the vertex $Q$ and turn it until the arm $QP$ lies along the $0$ line. All three angles share the arm $QP$, so one $0$ line serves all three.
$2$. Read the scale where each arm crosses it: $QR$ at $45^\circ$, $QS$ at $100^\circ$ and $QT$ at $150^\circ$.
$3$. So $\angle PQR = 45^\circ$, $\angle PQS = 100^\circ$ and $\angle PQT = 150^\circ$.
$4$. Check the order: an arm further from $QP$ must read a bigger number, and $45^\circ < 100^\circ < 150^\circ$.
Answer: $\angle PQR = 45^\circ$, $\angle PQS = 100^\circ$, $\angle PQT = 150^\circ$

Where are the angles?
1. Angles in a clock: a. The hands of a clock make different angles at different times. At 1 o'clock, the angle between the hands is 30°. Why? b. What will be the angle at 2 o'clock? And at 4 o'clock? 6 o'clock? c. Explore other angles made by the hands of a clock.

content.text:
1. Predict first: the hands of a clock make an angle at 5 o'clock. How many degrees is it?
2. The 12 hours cut the full turn of 360° into 12 equal parts, so each hour is 360 ÷ 12 = 30°.
3. At 5 o'clock the hands are 5 hours apart, so the angle is 5 × 30 = 150°.

content.text:
Worked example: What is the angle between the hands of a clock at 5 o'clock?
1. A full turn of the clock face is 360 degrees and it has 12 hours, so one hour is 360 ÷ 12 = 30 degrees.
2. At 5 o'clock the hands are 5 hours apart, so the angle is 5 × 30 = 150 degrees.
Answer: 150 degrees

content.text:
{{DIAGRAM:M3.S27.T27.C144.IMG1}}
$1$. A clock face is one full turn of $360^\circ$, cut by the $12$ numbers into $12$ equal gaps.
$2$. One gap is $360 \div 12 = 30$ degrees. At $1\text{ o'clock}$ the hands are $1$ gap apart, so the angle is $1 \times 30^\circ = 30^\circ$.
$3$. At $2\text{ o'clock}$ the hands are $2$ gaps apart: $2 \times 30^\circ = 60^\circ$.
$4$. At $4\text{ o'clock}$ the hands are $4$ gaps apart: $4 \times 30^\circ = 120^\circ$.
$5$. At $6\text{ o'clock}$ the hands are $6$ gaps apart: $6 \times 30^\circ = 180^\circ$.
$6$. Other hours work the same way: at $3\text{ o'clock}$, $3 \times 30^\circ = 90^\circ$.
$7$. At $9\text{ o'clock}$, $9 \times 30^\circ = 270^\circ$ one way round, and the other way round is $360^\circ - 270^\circ = 90^\circ$.
Answer: $(a)$: The clock's $360^\circ$ is divided into $12$ equal parts, so the angle between two successive numbers is $\frac{360}{12} = 30^\circ$. $(b)$: $2\text{ o'clock} = 60^\circ$, $4\text{ o'clock} = 120^\circ$, $6\text{ o'clock} = 180^\circ$. $(c)$: e.g. $3\text{ o'clock} = 90^\circ$, $9\text{ o'clock} = 270^\circ$.
steps: A clock face is one full turn of 360°, cut by the 12 numbers into 12 equal gaps.
One gap is 360 ÷ 12 = 30 degrees. At 1 o'clock the hands are 1 gap apart, so the angle is 1 × 30° = 30°.
At 2 o'clock the hands are 2 gaps apart: 2 × 30° = 60°.
At 4 o'clock the hands are 4 gaps apart: 4 × 30° = 120°.
At 6 o'clock the hands are 6 gaps apart: 6 × 30° = 180°.
Other hours work the same way: at 3 o'clock, 3 × 30° = 90°.
At 9 o'clock, 9 × 30° = 270° one way round, and the other way round is 360° − 270° = 90°.

content.text: The angle of a door: Is it possible to express the amount by which a door is opened using an angle? What will be the vertex of the angle and what will be the arms of the angle?
content.q_figure: A view from above of a door standing partly open in its wall.
content.question: The angle of a door: Is it possible to express the amount by which a door is opened using an angle? What will be the vertex of the angle and what will be the arms of the angle?
content.question_tex: The angle of a door: Is it possible to express the amount by which a door is opened using an angle? What will be the vertex of the angle and what will be the arms of the angle?
content.publication_text: The angle of a door: Is it possible to express the amount by which a door is opened using an angle? What will be the vertex of the angle and what will be the arms of the angle?

content.text:
{{DIAGRAM:M3.S27.T27.C146.IMG1}}
$1$. The door turns about the place where it meets the wall, the hinge, and this place does not move.
$2$. The two lines that make the opening are the edge of the door and the wall, so they are the two arms.
$3$. Open the door wider: the opening between its edge and the wall grows, so the amount a door is open is an angle.
$4$. Check with the closed door: its edge lies along the wall, so there is no opening.
Answer: Yes. The vertex is the point where the door meets the wall (the hinge); the arms are the edge of the door and the wall.

content.text: Vidya is enjoying her time on the swing. She notices that the greater the angle with which she starts the swinging, the greater is the speed she achieves on her swing. But where is the angle? Are you able to see any angle?
content.q_figure: A girl sitting on a swing that hangs from a tree branch.
content.question: Vidya is enjoying her time on the swing. She notices that the greater the angle with which she starts the swinging, the greater is the speed she achieves on her swing. But where is the angle? Are you able to see any angle?

content.publication_text: Vidya is enjoying her time on the swing. She notices that the greater the angle with which she starts the swinging, the greater is the speed she achieves on her swing. But where is the angle? Are you able to see any angle?

content.text:
{{DIAGRAM:M3.S27.T27.C148.IMG1}}
$1$. An angle shows a turn: one arm is where the turn starts and the other arm is where it ends, and the arms meet at the vertex.
$2$. Fix one arm at the position where the swing starts; it begins at the point where the swing hangs.
$3$. Watch how high the swing goes on one side before it comes back.
$4$. Draw the second arm from the hanging point to that highest position; the two arms make the angle.
$5$. Check with what Vidya noticed: the further back she starts, the greater the angle and the greater the speed.
Answer: The angle is not drawn, but fix one arm at the position where she starts swinging (initial position); the angle is between that position and the position where she attains the greatest swing on one side.

content.text: Here is a toy with slanting slabs attached to its sides; the greater the angles or slopes of the slabs, the faster the balls roll. Can angles be used to describe the slopes of the slabs? What are the arms of each angle? Which arm is visible and which is not?
content.q_figure: A toy with slanting slabs fixed to its sides and balls rolling down them.
content.question: Here is a toy with slanting slabs attached to its sides; the greater the angles or slopes of the slabs, the faster the balls roll. Can angles be used to describe the slopes of the slabs? What are the arms of each angle? Which arm is visible and which is not?

content.text:
{{DIAGRAM:M3.S27.T27.C150.IMG1}}
$1$. Look at one slab: its slanting edge is one arm of an angle, and it can be seen on the toy.
$2$. The second arm starts at the top of the slab and goes straight across, level with the ground; this top horizontal ray is not drawn, so it is not visible. The two arms make an angle.
$3$. Compare two slabs: a gentle slab makes a small angle and a steeper slab makes a larger angle.
$4$. Check with the balls: the slab with the larger angle makes the ball roll faster, so a larger angle means a greater slope.
Answer: Yes, a larger angle means a greater slope. The edges of the slabs are arms of the angles; the top horizontal ray is not visible, the slab edges are.

content.text:
{{DIAGRAM:M3.S27.T27.C152.IMG1}}
$1$. Sample answer: the horizontal line touching the insects is one arm of the angle.
$2$. Draw a line along the rotated insect; this line is the other arm.
$3$. The two arms meet at the point that does not move when the insect turns; this point of rotation on the line is the vertex, and the arc between the arms shows the amount of rotation.
$4$. Check by turning the insect back: the arc shrinks to nothing, because the two arms lie on each other.
Answer: Yes. Open-ended. E.g. the horizontal line is one arm and the line along the rotated insect is the other arm, with the vertex at the point of rotation on the line.

topics.summary: To draw an angle, draw one arm, put the protractor centre on the vertex with the arm on 0, mark the measure, and join.

content.text:
Vidya wants to draw a 30° angle and name it ∠TIN using a protractor.
In ∠TIN, I will be the vertex, IT and IN will be the arms of the angle. Keeping one arm, say IN, as the reference (base), the other arm IT should take a turn of 30°.
Step 1: We begin with the base and draw ray IN:
Step 2: We will place the centre point of the protractor on I and align IN to the 0 line.
Step 3: Now, starting from 0, count your degrees (0, 10, 30) up to 30 on the protractor. Mark point T at the label 30°.
Step 4: Using a ruler join the point I and T. ∠TIN = 30° is the required angle.

content.text:
This is an angle guessing game! Play this game with your classmates by making two teams, Team 1 and Team 2. Here are the instructions and rules for the game:
Team 1 secretly choose an angle measure, for example, 49° and makes an angle with that measure using a protractor without Team 2 being able to see it.
Team 2 now gets to look at the angle. They have to quickly discuss and guess the number of degrees in the angle (without using a protractor!).
Team 1 now demonstrates the true measure of the angle with a protractor.
Team 2 scores the number of points that is the absolute difference in degrees between their guess and the correct measure. For example, if Team 2 guesses 39°, then they score 10 points (49° to 39°).
Each team gets five turns. The winner is the team with the lowest score!
We now change the rules of the game a bit. Play this game with your classmates by again making two teams, Team 1 and Team 2. Here are the instructions and rules:
Team 1 announces to all, an angle measure, e.g., 34°.
A player from Team 2 must draw that angle on the board without using a protractor. Other members of Team 2 can help the player by speaking words like 'Make it bigger!' or 'Make it smaller!'.
A player from Team 1 measures the angle with a protractor for all to see.
Team 2 scores the number of points that is the absolute difference in degrees between Team 2's angle size and the intended angle size. For example, if player's angle from Team 2 is measured to be 25°, then Team 2 scores 9 points (34° to 25°).
Each team gets five turns. The winner is again the team with the lowest score.
Teacher's Note: These games are important to play to build intuition about angles and their measures. Return to this game at least once or twice on different days to build practice in estimating angles. Note that these games can also be played between pairs of students.

content.text:
1. Predict first: Team 1 draws an angle without showing it. Can Team 2 guess within a few degrees?
2. Guess, measure with the protractor, and score by how close you were. Closer guesses score more.
3. Keep the benchmark angles in mind: a right angle is 90°, half of it is 45°, and a straight angle is 180°. Guessing is practice for the eye, and the protractor gives the exact number.

content.text:
{{DIAGRAM:M4.S30.T30.C162.IMG1}}
$1$. Draw a base ray with its vertex at one end.
$2$. Place the centre of the protractor on the vertex and turn it until the base ray lies along the $0$ line.
$3$. Read the scale that starts at $0$ on the base ray, count up to the size needed and mark a point there. For $112^\circ$, go to $110^\circ$ and then count $2$ small marks more.
$4$. Join the mark to the vertex with a ruler. Do this for $110^\circ$, $40^\circ$, $75^\circ$, $112^\circ$ and $134^\circ$.
$5$. Check by eye: $40^\circ$ and $75^\circ$ are less than $90^\circ$, so they look narrower than a square corner; $110^\circ$, $112^\circ$ and $134^\circ$ are more than $90^\circ$, so they look wider, and $134^\circ$ is the widest.
Answer: Draw each angle with the protractor (base ray on the $0$ line, mark the point at the required reading, join to the vertex).

topics.summary: Under 90° is acute, 90° is right, between 90° and 180° is obtuse, 180° is straight, and between 180° and 360° is reflex.

content.text:
We have read about different types of angles in this chapter. We have seen that a straight angle is 180° and a right angle is 90°. How can other types of angles, acute and obtuse, be described in terms of their degree measures?
Acute Angle: Angles that are smaller than the right angle, i.e., less than 90° and are greater than 0°, are called acute angles.
Obtuse Angle: Angles that are greater than the right angle and less than the straight angle, i.e., greater than 90° and less than 180°, are called obtuse angles.

content.text:
1. Predict first: an angle measures 120°. Is it acute, right or obtuse?
2. Compare the measure with 90° and 180°. Less than 90° is acute, exactly 90° is right, and more than 90° and less than 180° is obtuse.
3. 90° is right and not obtuse, and 180° is a straight angle.

content.text:
Worked example: Name each angle as acute, right, obtuse or straight: 35°, 90°, 120°, 180°.
1. 35° is less than 90°, so it is acute.
2. 90° is exactly a quarter turn, so it is a right angle.
3. 120° is more than 90° and less than 180°, so it is obtuse.
4. 180° is a half turn, so it is a straight angle.
Answer: 35° is acute, 90° is right, 120° is obtuse and 180° is straight.

content.text:

Reflex angle: Angles that are greater than the straight angle and less than the whole angle, i.e., greater than 180° and less than 360°, are called reflex angles.

content.text:
1. Predict first: an angle opens past a straight angle. What do we call it, and how can we measure it with a protractor that stops at 180°?
2. An angle of more than 180° and less than 360° is a reflex angle.
3. Measure the smaller angle on the other side and take it from a full turn. If it is 100°, the reflex angle is 360 − 100 gives 260°.

2. The reflex angle is 360 − 100 gives 260 degrees.
Answer: 260 degrees

media.description: Four angles at the point T are read on a protractor, and each reading is compared with ninety and one hundred eighty degrees to give its name. The last angle has the same arms as the third but goes the long way round, so it is the rest of the full turn.

video_script.why: The child reads each angle on a protractor, names it by comparing with ninety and one hundred eighty degrees, and finds the long way round angle from the full turn.

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This is a question from your book about measuring angles.
Use a protractor to find the measure of each angle.

<bookmark mark='fig'/>A protractor sits on the point T.
<bookmark mark='four'/>Four angles are marked, P T R, P T Q, P T W and W T P.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>What does each one measure, and what is its name?

$1$. Sample answer: join $A$ to a grid point with a straight line; this line is the first arm of each angle, so every angle starts at $A$.
$2$. Acute angle: join $A$ to a grid point so that the opening is smaller than a square corner, which is a right angle of $90^\circ$.
$3$. Obtuse angle: join $A$ to a grid point so that the opening is wider than a square corner but narrower than a straight line $(180^\circ)$.
$4$. Reflex angle: take two arms from $A$ and mark the angle the long way round, past the straight line, so it is more than $180^\circ$.
$5$. Mark each angle with a curve at $A$, and check by laying a square corner and a straight edge on it.
Answer: Open-ended constructions on dot grids (join $A$ to other grid points to form the required type of angle).

content.text:
$1$. Put the centre of the protractor on the vertex $T$ and the $0$ line along the arm $TP$, then read the scale where each arm crosses it.
$2$. $TR$ reads $30^\circ$ and $TQ$ reads $60^\circ$, so $\angle PTR = 30^\circ$ and $\angle PTQ = 60^\circ$; both are less than $90^\circ$, so both are acute.
$3$. $TW$ reads $102^\circ$, so $\angle PTW = 102^\circ$, which is more than $90^\circ$ and less than $180^\circ$, so it is obtuse.
$4$. $\angle WTP$ has the same arms but goes the long way round, so $\angle WTP = 360^\circ - 102^\circ = 258^\circ$.
$5$. Check: $\angle PTW + \angle WTP = 102^\circ + 258^\circ = 360^\circ$, a full turn, and $258^\circ$ is more than $180^\circ$, so $\angle WTP$ is reflex.
Answer: $(a)$: $\angle PTR = 30^\circ$ (acute), $(b)$: $\angle PTQ = 60^\circ$ (acute), $(c)$: $\angle PTW = 102^\circ$ (obtuse), $(d)$: $\angle WTP = 258^\circ$ (reflex).

Classify these angles as acute, right, obtuse or reflex angles. $(a)$: angle $a$ (two arms meeting at a point on the right); $(b)$: angle $b$ (large arc); $(c)$: angle $c$; $(d)$: angle $d$; $(e)$: angle $e$; $(f)$: angle $f$ (arc drawn as a circle around the vertex)
{{DIAGRAM:M4.S32.T32.C175.IMG1}}

content.text:
$1$. Sample answer: estimate each angle by eye first. Lay a square corner $(90^\circ)$ and a straight edge $(180^\circ)$ on it and see whether the opening is smaller, about equal or bigger.
$2$. Measure: put the centre of the protractor on the vertex, lay the $0$ line along one arm and read the scale where the other arm crosses it. If the angle goes past a straight line, read the smaller side and take it from $360^\circ$.
$3$. Name the kind by comparing the measure with $90^\circ$ and $180^\circ$: less than $90^\circ$ is acute, $90^\circ$ is right, more than $90^\circ$ and less than $180^\circ$ is obtuse, and more than $180^\circ$ is reflex.
$4$. Check that each estimate is close to its measure and that the kind matches how the opening looks.
$5$. From the picture: angle $a$ is acute, angles $b$ and $c$ are obtuse, angle $d$ is acute, angle $e$ is about a right angle (or slightly obtuse) and angle $f$ is reflex.
Answer: Estimate first, then measure each of the six angles and classify (from the picture: $a$ is acute, $b$ is obtuse, $c$ is obtuse, $d$ is acute, $e$ is about a right angle or slightly obtuse, $f$ is reflex).

content.text: The Ashoka Chakra has $24$ spokes. What is the degree measure of the angle between two spokes next to each other? What is the largest acute angle formed between two spokes?
content.q_figure: The Ashoka Chakra, a wheel with 24 equal spokes.

content.text:
$1$. $360 \div 24 = 15$
$2$. Multiples of $15$ below $90$ are $15$, $30$, $45$, $60$, $75$; the largest is $75$
Answer: $15^\circ$ between neighbouring spokes; the largest acute angle between two spokes is $75^\circ$.

content.text: Puzzle: Here is an acute angle. If you double its measure, you get an acute angle. If you triple its measure, you will get an acute angle again. If you quadruple (four times) its measure, you will get an acute angle yet again! But if you multiply its measure by $5$, you will get an obtuse angle measure. What are the possibilities for its measure?

If you quadruple (four times) its measure, you will get an acute angle yet again! But if you multiply its measure by $5$, you will get an obtuse angle measure. What are the possibilities for its measure?

content.text:
$1$. $4 \times$ measure $< 90$, so measure $< 22.5$
$2$. $5 \times$ measure $> 90$, so measure $> 18$
$3$. Whole degrees between $18$ and $22.5$: $19$, $20$, $21$, $22$
Answer: The acute angle can be $19^\circ$, $20^\circ$, $21^\circ$ and $22^\circ$ (whole-number degrees).

topics.summary: A point marks a place, a ray and a line go on, an angle is a turn measured in degrees, and angles are named by their measure.

content.text:
A point determines a location. It is denoted by a capital letter.
A line segment corresponds to the shortest distance between two points. The line segment joining points S and T is denoted by ST (with a bar over it).
A line is obtained when a line segment like ST is extended on both sides indefinitely; it is denoted by ST (with a double arrow over it) or sometimes by a single small letter like m.
A ray is a portion of a line starting at a point D and going in one direction indefinitely. It is denoted by DP (with an arrow over it) where P is another point on the ray.
An angle can be visualised as two rays starting from a common starting point. Two rays OP and OM form the angle ∠POM (also called ∠MOP); here, O is called the vertex of the angle, and the rays OP and OM are called the arms of the angle.
The size of an angle is the amount of rotation or turn needed about the vertex to rotate one ray of the angle onto the other ray of the angle.
The sizes of angles can be measured in degrees. One full rotation or turn is considered as 360 degrees and denoted as 360°.
Degree measures of angles can be measured using a protractor.
Angles can be straight (180°), right (90°), acute (more than 0° and less than 90°), obtuse (more than 90° and less than 180°), and reflex (more than 180° and less than 360°).

content.text:
1. Predict first: a line, a ray and a segment all lie along the same path. How do they differ?
2. A segment has two ends, a ray has one end, and a line has none. An angle is the turn between two rays at a vertex, and its measure is in degrees: 90° is a right angle, and 360° is a full turn.
3. Still open for you: can you draw an angle of 135° and name its type before you measure it?
