modules.module_name: Drawing Angles and Types of Angles
modules.module_summary: A protractor also draws an angle of a given size. Every angle is acute, right, obtuse, straight or reflex by its measure, and the summary closes the chapter.

objectives.objective_text: Students mark a point with a sharp pencil tip, label the dot with a capital letter, and see a folded crease as a line segment with two end points.
Students compare routes between two points and conclude that the straight one is the shortest and is the line segment AB.
Students recall that a point marks an exact place and that the line segment is the shortest path between two points, and give an example of each from around them.
Students explain why a complete line cannot be drawn, say that two points fix exactly one line, and name a line through two points.
Students recognise a ray as a part of a line with one starting point, and write its name with the starting point first.
Students name the points, line segments, rays and lines in a figure, draw a figure from a description, and say whether two names of a ray are the same.
Students mark the two arms and the vertex of the angle in a book cover, a compass, scissors and a hinged object.
Students see that the size of an angle is the amount one arm turns about the vertex, so opening the cover more makes a greater angle.
Students name angles with three letters with the vertex in the middle, find the arms and vertex in pictures, and count the angles formed by three or four points.
Students compare two labelled angles by placing one over the other with the vertices together and one arm over one arm.
Students see that two angles are equal when they fit exactly on each other, and use the idea to compare other things.
Students place a transparent circle on an angle, mark where the arms cross it, and compare two angles by where the second arm meets the circle.
Students drag one angle over another on the tool, say which is greater or whether they are equal, and give a reason.
Students make rotating arms, order them by superimposition, and find the one that passes through a slit of the same angle.
Students explain why snipping the ends of the arms leaves an angle unchanged, and say how to really reduce it.
Students explain that the size of an angle is the turn between the arms and use a rotating arm to match an angle, whatever the length of the arms.
Students fold a straight angle so that its two arms overlap, and explain why the two angles formed are equal.
Students say that a right angle is a quarter of a full turn, and that it can be turned in any direction.
Students fold a paper on the tool to make a straight angle, a right angle and a perpendicular crease, and find right angles on a grid and in the classroom.
Students sort angles into three groups by comparing each with a right angle, and name the groups acute, right and obtuse.
Students identify acute, right, obtuse and straight angles in figures, draw some in different orientations, say why the words acute and obtuse were chosen, and count acute angles in a pattern.
Students say that the angle measure is the number of 1° unit parts, and give the measure of a full turn, a straight angle and a right angle.
Students find the angle at the centre when a circle is cut into 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10 or 12 equal parts, and see why 360 is a handy number.
Students state that a full turn is 360 degrees, a straight angle is 180 degrees and a right angle is 90 degrees, and find the angle for equal cuts of a circle.
Students say why a protractor has two sets of numbers and count 1° units on an unlabelled one.
Students name every angle at a vertex with its measure, and find an angle between two arms by subtracting their two readings.
Students place the protractor centre on the vertex, set one arm on the 0 mark, and read the other arm directly.
Students count the 1° units between two arms on an unlabelled protractor, using 5s and 10s.
Students fold a circle into a semicircle and a quarter circle and work out 180° and 90° from the full turn.
Students fold again to get 45° and 22.5°, and say why all eight equal angles on the straight angle are 22.5° each.
Students name a fold that halves an angle as an angle bisector, and find the angle bisectors in the folded paper semicircle.
Students fold a paper semicircle on the tool and place the marks 0°, 22.5°, 45°, 67.5°, 90°, 112.5°, 135°, 157.5° and 180°.
Students find what went wrong in a student's protractor reading, say which check was missed, and mend the reading.
Students place the protractor on angles of different sizes and directions and read each one, find the angles in a classroom, and check that the three angles of a triangle add to 180°.
Students find the angle between the clock hands at an hour by splitting 360° into 12 equal parts.
Students find angles in clocks, a door, a swing, a toy and a rotated picture, and give each as a turn in degrees.
Students draw a given angle, such as ∠TIN of 30°, with a protractor, by marking the measure and joining.
Students guess and check angle sizes in two team games, and see how a good estimate comes from remembering 30°, 45°, 60° and 90°.
Students list every angle in a figure, draw angles of given sizes, and copy an angle by measuring it.
Students name an angle as acute, right, obtuse or straight by comparing its measure with 90 and 180.
Students say that an angle bigger than a straight angle and less than a full turn is reflex, and find its measure from the part of the turn that is left.
Students use the 180° straight angle to find an unknown neighbouring angle by subtracting the given one.
Students measure or estimate angles, classify each, draw angles of given sizes and build figures and letters from angle clues.
Students recall how lines, rays and angles are named, how an angle is measured and drawn, and what each type of angle is.

video_coverage.book_item: Book item: Fold a piece of paper and unfold it. Do you see a crease? (This gives the idea of a line segment. It has two end points, A and B.)
Book item: Mark any two points A and B on a sheet of paper. Try to connect A to B by various routes (Fig. 2.1). What is the shortest route from A to B?

Book item: Imagine that the line segment AB is extended beyond A in one direction and beyond B in the other direction without any end (Fig. 2.2). Do you think you can draw a complete picture of a line? No. Why?

Book item: Rihan marked a point on a piece of paper. How many lines can he draw that pass through the point? Sheetal marked two points on a piece of paper. How many different lines can she draw that pass through both of the points? Can you help Rihan and Sheetal find their answers? Rihan) How many lines can be drawn through one marked point? Sheetal) How many different lines through both of two marked points?

Book item: Name the line segments in Fig. 2.4. Which of the five marked points are on exactly one of the line segments? Which are on two of the line segments? (Fig. 2.4 is a zig-zag path L-M-P-Q-R: L to M, M to P, P to Q, Q to R.) a) Name the line segments. b) Points on exactly one segment c) Points on two segments

Book item: Name the rays shown in Fig. 2.5. Is T the starting point of each of these rays? (Fig. 2.5: from T one ray goes up-right through A; another goes right through N and then B.) a) Name the rays b) Is T the starting point of each?

Book item: Draw a rough figure and write labels appropriately to illustrate each of the following: a. OP and OQ (lines) meet at O. b. XY (ray) and PQ (line) intersect at point M. c. Line l contains points E and F but not point D. d. Point P lies on AB. a) Line OP and line OQ meet at O. b) Ray XY and line PQ intersect at point M. c) Line l contains E and F but not D. d) Point P lies on AB.

Book item: In Fig. 2.6, name: a. Five points b. A line c. Four rays d. Five line segments. (Fig. 2.6: a line passes through D, E, O, B; a ray from O goes through C; another ray from O goes straight up.) a) Five points b) A line c) Four rays d) Five line segments

Book item: Here is a ray OA (Fig. 2.7). It starts at O and passes through the point A. It also passes through the point B. a. Can you also name it as OB? Why? b. Can we write OA as AO? Why or why not? a) Can you also name it as OB? Why? b) Can we write OA as AO? Why or why not?
Book item: Vidya opens the cover of her book in six cases (Case 1 to Case 6). Do you see angles being made in each of these cases? Can you mark their arms and vertex?
Book item: In a compass or divider, we turn the arms to form an angle. The vertex is the point where the two arms are joined. Identify the arms and vertex of the angle.
Book item: A pair of scissors has two blades. When we open them (or 'turn them') to cut something, the blades form an angle. Identify the arms and the vertex of the angle.
Book item: Look at the pictures of spectacles, wallet and other common objects (a stapler, a hinged box, a box with an open flap). Identify the angles in them by marking out their arms and vertices.
Book item: Which angle is greater: the angle in Case 1 or the angle in Case 2?
Book item: Do you see how these angles are formed by turning one arm with respect to the other?

Book item: Can you find the angles in the given pictures? Draw the rays forming any one of the angles and name the vertex of the angle. (Pictures: a bicycle with points A, B, C, D and arrows marked on it, a wooden crate with slanting slats, a ladder, a bridge.)
Book item: Draw and label an angle with arms ST and SR.
Book item: Explain why ∠APB cannot be labelled as ∠P. (Figure: vertex P with three rays going through A (upper), B (middle) and C (lower).)
Book item: Name the angles marked in the given figure. (Figure: vertex T with rays to P, Q and R; curved marks drawn at T.)

Book item: Mark any three points on your paper that are not on one line. Label them A, B, C. Draw all possible lines going through pairs of these points. How many lines do you get? Name them. How many angles can you name using A, B, C? Write them down, and mark each of them with a curve as in Fig. 2.9. lines) How many lines? Name them. angles) How many angles using A, B, C?

Book item: Now mark any four points on your paper so that no three of them are on one line. Label them A, B, C, D. Draw all possible lines going through pairs of these points. How many lines do you get? Name them. How many angles can you name using A, B, C, D? Write them all down, and mark each of them with a curve as in Fig. 2.9. lines) How many lines? Name them. angles) How many angles using A, B, C, D?

Book item: Look at these animals opening their mouths (snake, fish, bird, crocodile). Do you see any angles here? If yes, mark the arms and vertex of each one. Some mouths are open wider than others; the more the turning of the jaws, the larger the angle! Can you arrange the angles in this picture from smallest to largest?
Book item: Here are some angles (four angles drawn with different openings and orientations). Label each of the angles. How will you compare them? Draw a few more angles; label them and compare.
Book item: Now consider ∠AOB and ∠XOY in the figure. Which is greater?
Book item: Where else do we use superimposition to compare?
Book item: Is it always easy to compare two angles?

Book item: A transparent circle is placed on the angle of the first crane with its centre at the vertex; A and B are marked where the arms cross the circle. The circle is then placed on the second crane's angle with the vertex at the centre and one arm through OA. Can you now tell which angle is bigger?
Book item: Which crane was making the bigger angle? If you can make a circular piece of transparent paper, try this method to compare the angles in Fig. 2.10 with each other.

Book item: Fold a rectangular sheet of paper, then draw a line along the fold created. Name and compare the angles formed between the fold and the sides of the paper. Make different angles by folding a rectangular sheet of paper and compare the angles. Which is the largest and smallest angle you made?

Book item: In each case, determine which angle is greater and why. a. ∠AOB or ∠XOY b. ∠AOB or ∠XOB c. ∠XOB or ∠XOC. Discuss with your friends on how you decided which one is greater. (Figure: O is the vertex; OA is vertical, OX and OY are slanting rays with OX steeper, B and C are on the same horizontal ray, B nearer O.) a) ∠AOB or ∠XOY b) ∠AOB or ∠XOB c) ∠XOB or ∠XOC
Book item: Which angle is greater: ∠XOY or ∠AOB? Give reasons. (Figure: vertex O; OX up-left, OA up-right, OY nearly horizontal slightly up, OB horizontal.)

Book item: Make several 'rotating arms' (two paper straws and a paper clip) with different angles between the arms. Arrange the angles you have made from smallest to largest by comparing and using superimposition.

Book item: Collect a number of rotating arms with different angles (do not rotate any of them). Take a cardboard and make an angle-shaped slit by tracing and cutting out the shape of one of the rotating arms. Now shuffle and mix up all the rotating arms. Can you identify which of the rotating arms will pass through the slit?
Book item: Challenge: Reduce this angle. (A girl snips the ends of the arms of a V-shaped rotating arm with scissors: 'Angle reduced.' The boy says 'The angle is still the same!')
Book item: Is it possible to draw OC such that the two angles (∠AOC and ∠COB, with ∠AOB a straight angle) are equal to each other in size?

Book item: Take a rectangular piece of paper and on one of its sides, mark the straight angle AOB. By folding, try to get a line (crease) passing through O that divides ∠AOB into two equal angles. How can it be done?
Book item: Justify why the two angles are equal. Is there a way to superimpose and check? Can this superimposition be done by folding?
Book item: If a straight angle is formed by half of a full turn, how much of a full turn will form a right angle?
Book item: How many right angles do the windows of your classroom contain? Do you see other right angles in your classroom?

Book item: Join A to other grid points in the figure by a straight line to get a straight angle. What are all the different ways of doing it? (Two dot grids of 7 columns by 6 rows. Left grid: A at row 3, column 4 and B at row 3, column 7 joined by a horizontal segment. Right grid: A at row 3, column 3 and B at row 5, column 5, joined by a diagonal segment through the dot at row 4, column 4.) left grid) Join A so that AB makes a straight angle right grid) Join A so that AB makes a straight angle

Book item: Now join A to other grid points in the figure by a straight line to get a right angle. What are all the different ways of doing it? Hint: Extend the line further as shown in the figure below. To get a right angle at A, we need to draw a line through it that divides the straight angle CAB into two equal parts. (Same two grids as Q2.) left grid) Join A to grid points so that the new segment is at right angles to AB right grid) Join A to grid points so that the new segment is at right angles to AB

Book item: Get a slanting crease on the paper. Now, try to get another crease that is perpendicular to the slanting crease. a. How many right angles do you have now? Justify why the angles are exact right angles. b. Describe how you folded the paper so that any other person who doesn't know the process can simply follow your description to get the right angle. a) How many right angles? Justify. b) Describe how you folded the paper.

Book item: Angles are classified in three groups as shown (a box with three columns of angle drawings). Right angles are shown in the second group. What could be the common feature of the other two groups?
Book item: Identify acute, right, obtuse and straight angles in the previous figures.
Book item: Make a few acute angles and a few obtuse angles. Draw them in different orientations.
Book item: Do you know what the words acute and obtuse mean? Acute means sharp and obtuse means blunt. Why do you think these words have been chosen?

Book item: Find out the number of acute angles in each of the figures below. What will be the next figure and how many acute angles will it have? Do you notice any pattern in the numbers? (Figures: (i) one triangle; (ii) the triangle divided into 4 small triangles; (iii) divided into 7 small triangles.) i) Acute angles in the first figure ii) Acute angles in the second figure iii) Acute angles in the third figure next) Next figure
Book item: What is the measure of a straight angle in degrees? What is the measure of a right angle in degrees?

Book item: The circle has been divided into 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10 and 12 parts below. What are the degree measures of the resulting angles? Write the degree measures down near the indicated angles.

Book item: Will these (the numbers written on the protractor) make it easier to read the angles? There are two sets of numbers on the protractor: one increasing from right to left and the other increasing from left to right. Why does it include two sets of numbers?
Book item: Name the different angles in the figure and write their measures.
Book item: Did you include angles such as ∠TOQ? Which set of markings did you use, inner or outer? What is the measure of ∠TOS?

Book item: Can you use the numbers marked to find the angle without counting the number of markings? Here, OT and OS pass through the numbers 20 and 55 on the outer scale. How many units of 1 degree are contained between these two arms? Can subtraction be used here?

Book item: Place the protractor so the centre is on the vertex of the angle. Align the protractor so that one of the arms passes through the 0° mark as in the picture below. What is the degree measure of ∠AOB?

Book item: Write the measures of the following angles: a. ∠KAL b. ∠WAL c. ∠TAK. (Worked in the book for a: the vertex coincides with the centre of the protractor, so the number of units of 1 degree between KA and AL gives ∠KAL = 30°. Follow-up: Making use of the medium sized and large sized marks, is it possible to count the number of units in 5s or 10s?) a) ∠KAL b) ∠WAL c) ∠TAK

Book item: Make your own protractor by paper folding. 1. Draw a circle of a convenient radius on a sheet of paper. Cut out the circle (Fig. 2.13). A circle or one full turn is 360°. 2. Fold the circle to get two equal halves and cut it through the crease to get a semicircle. Write '0°' in the bottom right corner of the semicircle. 3. Fold the semi-circular sheet in half as shown in Fig. 2.15 to form a quarter circle. 4. Fold the sheet again as shown in Figs. 2.16 and 2.17. 5. Continue with another half fold as shown in Fig. 2.18. 6. Unfold and mark the creases as OB, OC, ..., etc., as shown in Fig. 2.19 and Fig. 2.20.
Book item: The measure of half a circle is 1/2 of a full turn. So, the measure of half a turn = 1/2 of ____ = 180°. Thus, write 180° in the left bottom corner of the semicircle.

Book item: The measure of a quarter circle is 1/4 of a full turn. The measure of a 1/4 turn = 1/4 of 360° is ________. Or, the measure of a 1/4 turn = 1/2 of a half turn = 1/2 of 180° is ______. Thus, mark 90° at the top of the semicircle.

Book item: When folded, this is 1/8 of the circle, or 1/8 of a turn, or 1/8 of 360°, or 1/4 of 180° or 1/2 of 90° is ____________. The new creases give us measures of 45° and 180° − 45° = 135° as shown. Write 45° and 135° at the correct places on the new creases along the edge of the semicircle.
Book item: Continuing with another half fold as shown in Fig. 2.18, we get an angle of measure ____________.
Book item: In Fig. 2.19, we have ∠AOB = ∠BOC = ∠COD = ∠DOE = ∠EOF = ∠FOG = ∠GOH = ∠HOI = _____. Why?
Book item: Identify the angle bisectors in your handmade protractor. Try to make different angles using the concept of angle bisector through paper folding.

Book item: A student used a protractor to measure the angles as shown below. In each figure, identify the incorrect usage(s) of the protractor and discuss how the reading could have been made and think how it can be corrected. (Readings: ∠U = 35°, ∠V = 80°, ∠W = 70°, ∠X = 150°, ∠Y = 120°, ∠Z = 85°.)

Book item: Find the degree measures of the following angles using your protractor. (Three angles drawn, each with a small arc at vertex H.) first) angle at H between HI and HJ (I nearly straight up, J up to the right) second) narrow angle at H (G, I and J, K on the two long arms) third) angle at H with I at upper right and J at lower right
Book item: Find the degree measures of different angles in your classroom using your protractor.

Book item: Find the degree measures for the angles given below. Check if your paper protractor can be used here! first) angle at H between HI and HJ (left drawing) second) angle at H between HI and HJ (right drawing)
Book item: How can you find the degree measure of the angle given below using a protractor?
Book item: Measure and write the degree measures for each of the following angles: a, b, c, d, e, f. a) angle a b) angle b c) angle c d) angle d e) angle e f) angle f
Book item: Find the degree measures of ∠BXE, ∠CXE, ∠AXB and ∠BXC. a) ∠BXE b) ∠CXE c) ∠AXB d) ∠BXC
Book item: Find the degree measures of ∠PQR, ∠PQS and ∠PQT. a) ∠PQR b) ∠PQS c) ∠PQT
Book item: Make the paper craft as per the given instructions. Then, unfold and open the paper fully. Draw lines on the creases made and measure the angles formed.

Book item: Measure all three angles of the triangle shown in Fig. 2.21 (a), and write the measures down near the respective angles. Now add up the three measures. What do you get? Do the same for the triangles in Fig. 2.21 (b) and (c). Try it for other triangles as well, and then make a conjecture for what happens in general! We will come back to why this happens in a later year.

Book item: Angles in a clock: a. The hands of a clock make different angles at different times. At 1 o'clock, the angle between the hands is 30°. Why? b. What will be the angle at 2 o'clock? And at 4 o'clock? 6 o'clock? c. Explore other angles made by the hands of a clock. a) At 1 o'clock the angle between the hands is 30°. Why? b) Angle at 2, 4 and 6 o'clock c) Explore other angles made by the hands of a clock
Book item: The angle of a door: Is it possible to express the amount by which a door is opened using an angle? What will be the vertex of the angle and what will be the arms of the angle?

Book item: Vidya is enjoying her time on the swing. She notices that the greater the angle with which she starts the swinging, the greater is the speed she achieves on her swing. But where is the angle? Are you able to see any angle?

Book item: Here is a toy with slanting slabs attached to its sides; the greater the angles or slopes of the slabs, the faster the balls roll. Can angles be used to describe the slopes of the slabs? What are the arms of each angle? Which arm is visible and which is not?

Book item: Observe the images below where there is an insect and its rotated version. Can angles be used to describe the amount of rotation? How? What will be the arms of the angle and the vertex? Hint: Observe the horizontal line touching the insects.

Book item: Vidya wants to draw a 30° angle and name it ∠TIN using a protractor. In ∠TIN, I will be the vertex, IT and IN will be the arms of the angle. Keeping one arm, say IN, as the reference (base), the other arm IT should take a turn of 30°. Step 1: We begin with the base and draw ray IN. Step 2: We will place the centre point of the protractor on I and align IN to the 0 line. Step 3: Now, starting from 0, count your degrees (0, 10, 30) up to 30 on the protractor. Mark point T at the label 30°. Step 4: Using a ruler join the point I and T. ∠TIN = 30° is the required angle.

Book item: Angle guessing game with two teams. Team 1 secretly chooses an angle measure, for example 49°, and makes an angle with that measure using a protractor without Team 2 being able to see it. Team 2 now gets to look at the angle. They have to quickly discuss and guess the number of degrees in the angle (without using a protractor!). Team 1 now demonstrates the true measure of the angle with a protractor. Team 2 scores the number of points that is the absolute difference in degrees between their guess and the correct measure. For example, if Team 2 guesses 39°, then they score 10 points (49°−39°). Each team gets five turns. The winner is the team with the lowest score.

Book item: Same two teams, new rules. Team 1 announces to all an angle measure, e.g., 34°. A player from Team 2 must draw that angle on the board without using a protractor. Other members of Team 2 can help the player by speaking words like 'Make it bigger!' or 'Make it smaller!'. A player from Team 1 measures the angle with a protractor for all to see. Team 2 scores the number of points that is the absolute difference in degrees between Team 2's angle size and the intended angle size. For example, if the player's angle from Team 2 is measured to be 25°, then Team 2 scores 9 points (34°−25°). Each team gets five turns. The winner is again the team with the lowest score.

Book item: In Fig. 2.23, list all the angles possible. Did you find them all? Now, guess the measures of all the angles. Then, measure the angles with a protractor. Record all your numbers in a table. See how close your guesses are to the actual measures.
Book item: Use a protractor to draw angles having the following degree measures: a. 110° b. 40° c. 75° d. 112° e. 134° a) 110° b) 40° c) 75° d) 112° e) 134°
Book item: Draw an angle whose degree measure is the same as the angle given below. Also, write down the steps you followed to draw the angle.

Book item: In this figure, ∠TER = 80°. What is the measure of ∠BET? What is the measure of ∠SET? (Hint: Observe that ∠REB is a straight angle. Hence, the degree measure of ∠REB = 180° of which 80° is covered by ∠TER. A similar argument can be applied to find the measure of ∠SET.)

Book item: In each of the below grids, join A to other grid points in the figure by a straight line to get: a. An acute angle b. An obtuse angle c. A reflex angle. Mark the intended angles with curves to specify the angles. One has been done for you. a) An acute angle (two grids) b) An obtuse angle (two grids) c) A reflex angle (two grids)
Book item: Use a protractor to find the measure of each angle. Then classify each angle as acute, obtuse, right, or reflex. a. ∠PTR b. ∠PTQ c. ∠PTW d. ∠WTP a) ∠PTR b) ∠PTQ c) ∠PTW d) ∠WTP
Book item: Draw angles with the following degree measures: a. 140° b. 82° c. 195° d. 70° e. 35° a) 140° b) 82° c) 195° d) 70° e) 35°

Book item: Estimate the size of each angle and then measure it with a protractor: a, b, c, d, e, f. Classify these angles as acute, right, obtuse or reflex angles. a) angle a (two arms meeting at a point on the right) b) angle b (large arc) c) angle c d) angle d e) angle e f) angle f (arc drawn as a circle around the vertex)
Book item: Make any figure with three acute angles, one right angle and two obtuse angles.
Book item: Draw the letter 'M' such that the angles on the sides are 40° each and the angle in the middle is 60°.
Book item: Draw the letter 'Y' such that the three angles formed are 150°, 60° and 150°.
Book item: The Ashoka Chakra has 24 spokes. What is the degree measure of the angle between two spokes next to each other? What is the largest acute angle formed between two spokes?

Book item: Puzzle: I am an acute angle. If you double my measure, you get an acute angle. If you triple my measure, you will get an acute angle again. If you quadruple (four times) my measure, you will get an acute angle yet again! But if you multiply my measure by 5, you will get an obtuse angle measure. What are the possibilities for my measure?

chapter_approach.intro: The chapter follows the book's order. It starts from points, segments, lines and rays, then builds the angle as a turn, compares angles by laying one over another, and only then measures and draws them in degrees.

points.text: An angle is first seen as the amount one arm turns about a point, compared by laying angles over each other, and only afterwards given a size in degrees.
points.title: A turn first, a number later

points.text: Each idea gets its own topic: worked videos for the book's questions, a tool only where handling the angle is the idea, then the book's Figure it Out questions in a practice topic, each with its own video.
points.title: Concept, then practice, topic by topic

points.text: Paper folds make the straight angle, the right angle and a paper protractor, so the numbers on a protractor are understood and not just read.
points.title: Fold it, turn it, measure it

points.text: The common wrong ideas, such as 'longer arms make a bigger angle', are raised by Keeko and fixed with a turn or an overlap, never just a rule.
points.title: Keeko's doubts
